Characterising Classical Feedback Latency in Software-Based QEC Decoders

A four-weekend project of mine: I measured how long a software decoder takes to turn a syndrome into a correction, how often it misses the qubits' coherence deadline, and how much logical error each microsecond of delay costs.

Why I did this

A quantum error-correcting code only protects anything if the loop measure syndrome → decode → apply correction closes before the qubits decohere. Most simulations quietly assume the classical part is instant, and I wanted to know if that is fair. Take a dephasing time T₂ = 120 µs (a conservative figure for IBM superconducting qubits) and N = 3 syndrome rounds per logical cycle: each round's classical work must fit within τDD = T₂/N = 40 µs.

The question: does a decoder running as ordinary software meet that deadline, how often does it miss, and what does a late correction cost? The violation rate VR(τ) = P(L > τ) is compared with the surface-code threshold pth ≈ 1% (Fowler et al. 2012), used here as an error budget.

Four research questions

RQ1
Violation rate
What is VR(τ) across deadlines from 10 ns to 100 µs, and where does it cross 1%?
RQ2
Tail behaviour
Is the latency tail light (log-normal) or heavy (power law)?
RQ3
Device noise
Does the code still help under realistic device noise, and what does feedback latency cost?
RQ4
Implementation tier
How much does a compiled C decoder improve on pure Python?

What's in the project

  • C1 — Latency dataset. 10,000 timed decode cycles per tier (Python, C via ctypes, modelled bare-metal), with measured timer floors and a 10-run repeat study, saved as JSON.
  • C2 — Statistical framework. Exact Clopper–Pearson intervals for VR(τ), bootstrap intervals for τ*, Anderson–Darling and Kolmogorov–Smirnov fits, the Hill tail index, and Mann–Whitney U with rank-biserial effect size.
  • C3 — Device-level protocol. A bare qubit, offline decoding and real-time feed-forward compared on one fixed physical layout, with Wilson intervals and χ² tests; runs locally on calibration replicas or on IBM hardware.
  • C4 — Threshold crossover. τ* = the deadline where VR(τ*) = 1%, per tier, with its headroom against τDD.
  • C5 — Latency sweep. Logical error as a function of decoder wait, connecting the measured latency tail to its cost in fidelity.

Run it yourself

Clone the repository and run two scripts. setup.sh makes a virtual environment with the pinned versions below, and run_all.sh reruns every experiment into outputs/ (about 6 minutes on 2 cores). pytest runs the unit tests. Weekends 1–3 and the local Weekend 4 runs need no IBM account. On Windows, use WSL, because the C decoder needs gcc and a POSIX clock.

git clone <this repository> qec-decoder-latency
cd qec-decoder-latency
bash setup.sh
bash run_all.sh
source qec-env/bin/activate && pytest
IBM Quantum access (Weekend 4 hardware only). The platform moved to quantum.cloud.ibm.com in 2025, and the old ibm_quantum channel was removed in qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.41. Create an API key there and save it once with python src/save_ibm_account.py (it asks for the key, so the key never sits in a file). The free Open Plan includes 10 minutes of quantum-computer time per 28 days.

TheoryRead once, refer back often

Theoretical background

The mathematics that connects qubit coherence to a classical timing budget.

1. Coherence and the decoherence deadline

A qubit loses information through two channels. Energy relaxation (T₁) takes |1⟩ to |0⟩; dephasing (T₂) scrambles the phase of a superposition without changing populations. Physics requires T₂ ≤ 2T₁. A state prepared in |+⟩, left idle for time t and rotated back with a Hadamard gate is still |+⟩ with probability

F(t) = ½ + ½ · exp(−t / T₂)[1] Ramsey decay

A ground-state qubit |0⟩ shows no decay at all under relaxation, which is why Experiment 1.1 must start from |+⟩. With N syndrome rounds per logical cycle, each round's classical work has a budget of

τDD = T₂ / N = 120 µs / 3 = 40 µs[2] decoherence deadline

2. The 3-qubit bit-flip code

|0⟩L = |000⟩ · |1⟩L = |111⟩ · |ψ⟩L = α|000⟩ + β|111⟩[3] encoding

The code corrects any single X (bit-flip) error and is blind to Z (phase-flip) errors; the surface code handles both with a two-dimensional lattice of checks. Two ancillas measure the parities Z₀Z₁ and Z₁Z₂ without measuring the data qubits, so a superposition survives the check. Qiskit prints classical bits right to left, so the syndrome string reads (Z₀Z₁)(Z₁Z₂):

Syndrome stringZ₀Z₁Z₁Z₂DiagnosisCorrection
0000no errornone
1010qubit 0 flippedX on q₀
1111qubit 1 flippedX on q₁
0101qubit 2 flippedX on q₂

If each data qubit flips independently with probability p, the logical qubit fails when two or three flip:

PL(p) = 3p²(1 − p) + p³ = 3p² − 2p³[4] logical error

The code beats a bare qubit for every p < ½, by a factor of about 1/(3p) when p is small.

3. Violation rate and the threshold budget

VR(τ) = P(L > τ) ≈ (1/n) Σ 1[Li > τ][5] violation rate
τ* = inf { τ : VR(τ) ≤ pth } = the 99th percentile when pth = 1%[6] threshold crossover

Comparing VR with pth ≈ 1% treats a missed deadline as one more error event. That is a modelling choice, not a theorem: pth is a per-operation physical error rate, used here as a budget. A tier is viable when τ* ≤ τDD; Weekend 4 shows why that condition is necessary but far from sufficient.

VR is a binomial proportion, so its interval comes from the exact Clopper–Pearson method. When 0 of n cycles miss, the 95% upper bound is about 3.7/n (0.037% for n = 10,000), whereas a bootstrap interval collapses to [0, 0].

4. Latency distribution models

  • Log-normal: ln L ~ N(µ, σ²). Multiplicative small delays (cache misses, branch mispredictions) produce it; every moment is finite.
  • Power-law tail: P(L > x) ~ x−α. The Hill estimator measures α from the largest observations: α > 4 light, 2 < α ≤ 4 moderate, α ≤ 2 heavy (infinite variance).
  • Mixture: a fast body plus a rare, separate population of long stalls (scheduler preemption, interrupts, hypervisor steal time). Neither model above predicts it; it appears as a plateau on a log-log survival plot. This is what the measurements in Weekend 3 show.

Weekend 1Coherence and error sensitivity≈ 5 hours

Physical foundation

Before timing anything I wanted to see the clock I'm racing: a Ramsey measurement recovers T₂ from the noise model, and a Pauli experiment shows which errors a superposition can actually feel.

Shared figure style

Every plotting script imports this small module, so all figures share fonts, colours and file formats (a vector PDF and a PNG preview). Its three series colours stay distinguishable under the common forms of colour-vision deficiency.

Experiment 1.1 — Ramsey coherence decay

Prepare |+⟩, idle for d gates of 50 ns each, rotate back and measure. Only the idle gates carry thermal relaxation, so the idle time t = d × 50 ns is exact and the one-parameter fit of equation [1] returns T₂ directly. Twenty-five idle times span 0–300 µs, enough to see the full decay.

Reference run

Fitted T₂ = 121.5 ± 1.3 µs against a model value of 120 µs (1.2 standard errors). At the 40 µs deadline the fidelity is 0.860; after a full three-round cycle (120 µs) it is 0.686.

Why |+⟩ and not |0⟩. Thermal relaxation pulls qubits toward |0⟩, so a qubit that starts there never decays. My first version did exactly that, and the fit ran off to the optimiser's bound: T₂ = 44,142 µs.

Experiment 1.2 — Which Pauli errors does |+⟩ feel?

Insert one idle gate between two Hadamards and give it a Pauli channel: operator P with probability p, identity otherwise. X leaves |+⟩ unchanged; Y and Z turn it into |−⟩. The noise must sit on the idle gate only: on the Hadamards, an X error after the second one flips the readout and fakes a sensitivity to X.

Reference run

X: survival 1.000 at every p. Y and Z: every point within 0.0123 of 1 − p. The bit-flip code corrects exactly the error |+⟩ cannot feel and is blind to the ones it can, which is why codes that protect superpositions also need phase checks.

Weekend 1 checklist

  • Fitted T₂ within about 2 standard errors of 120 µs
  • X curve flat at 1.0; Y and Z on the line 1 − p
  • fig1_coherence_decay.pdf, fig2_pauli_sensitivity.pdf, w1_coherence.json, w1_pauli.json saved
Weekend 2Syndrome extraction and decoding≈ 6 hours

The 3-qubit code in full

Build the code, check that its decoder picks the right correction under noise, and confirm that it actually suppresses errors.

Experiment 2.1 — The BitFlipCode class

Each cycle encodes |1⟩L, injects no error or one X error at random, extracts the syndrome on two ancillas under thermal-relaxation noise, runs one shot, and decodes. Only the decode step sits between the two clock reads. Every cycle gets a fresh simulator seed: Aer seeds shot k with seed + k, so one fixed seed would replay identical noise every cycle.

Reference run · 10,000 cycles

The decoder chose the matching correction in 98.61% of cycles (Wilson 95% CI 98.36–98.82%). Failures spread evenly over every injected case, so they come from relaxation during the six 500 ns CNOTs, not from the table.

Injected ↓ / decoded →noneq₀q₁q₂Correct
none2,49912111298.62%
q₀152,48223798.22%
q₁1072,4591098.91%
q₂15892,42198.70%

Decode time inside the full cycle: median 716 ns, P99 1,193 ns. One cycle took 104 µs and missed the 40 µs deadline. Weekend 3 isolates that tail.

Experiment 2.2 — Logical versus physical error

Does the code help? Give each data qubit an independent X error with probability p, extract the syndrome, correct in real time with if_test, and read out. Theory (equation [4]) predicts 3p² − 2p³.

Reference run · 11 values of p × 100,000 shots

All 11 points contain the theory value inside their 95% interval. At p = 1% the logical failure rate is 0.039% (95% CI 0.029–0.053%), 25× fewer failures than a bare qubit; at p = 10% the gain is 3.6×; at p = 50% it is gone.

Weekend 2 checklist

  • Syndrome table verified against the confusion matrix: no off-diagonal pattern
  • Every logical-error point contains 3p² − 2p³ inside its 95% interval
  • w2_latencies.json and w2_logical_error.json saved
Weekend 3Timing analysis≈ 6 hours

The latency distribution

How long does decoding take, how often is it late, and what shape does the tail have?

Experiment 3.1 — Distribution fitting

Fit log-normal, gamma and Weibull distributions to the Weekend 2 latencies and estimate the tail index. Kolmogorov–Smirnov p-values are optimistic once parameters are fitted from the same data, so compare the KS distance D; with 10,000 samples, every simple family is formally rejected.

Reference run

Closest family by KS distance: log-normal (D = 0.103, against 0.177 for gamma and 0.333 for Weibull). Anderson–Darling still rejects exact log-normality (A² = 245, p ≤ 0.01). Hill index on the top 5%: α = 4.09, at the light/moderate boundary.

Experiment 3.2 — Three tiers, timer floors and VR(τ)

The same look-up table runs as a Python dictionary and as compiled C called through ctypes; a modelled bare-metal tier (Cortex-M7, 41-cycle WCET = 85.4 ns, 5% jitter) sets the scale. Each measured tier also records its timer floor: two clock reads with nothing between them. Build the C library first:

mkdir -p build
gcc -O2 -shared -fPIC -o build/qec_decode.so src/qec_decode.c    # run_all.sh does this for you
Reference run · 10,000 timed cycles per tier after 1,000 warm-up
TierMedianTimer floorP99P99.9MaxMisses at 40 µsVR@40 µs, 95% CI
Python113 ns63 ns268 ns481 ns41.8 µs1 of 10,0000.01% [0.0003, 0.056]
C extension31 ns26 ns46 ns113 ns23.0 µs0 of 10,0000% [0, 0.037]
Bare-metal (modelled)85 ns—95 ns99 ns0.10 µs0 of 10,0000% [0, 0.037]

Typical decodes are 350× (Python) and 1,300× (C) inside the budget, and most of what both tiers measure is the clock itself: about 50 ns and 5 ns of real work. The risk sits in a separate population of stalls (7 Python cycles and 1 C cycle over 1 µs) that strike both tiers alike.

Repeat study (--repeats 10, 100,000 further cycles per tier): no misses in either tier. Pooled over 110,000 cycles, Python's VR@40 µs is at most 0.0051% and C's at most 0.0034% (95% upper bounds). Python medians ranged 113–148 ns and worst stalls 11–42 µs between runs, so single-run maxima on a shared machine are not reproducible numbers.

Exact versus bootstrap intervals. With one observed miss, the bootstrap interval for VR@40 µs is [0, 0.03%] and the exact interval is [0.0003, 0.056%]: resampling cannot invent misses it never saw. With zero misses the bootstrap collapses to [0, 0]. Use exact binomial intervals for rare events.

Weekend 3 checklist

  • qec_decode.so builds without warnings
  • Timer floors recorded; net decode cost = median − floor
  • Repeat study run; misses pooled with an exact interval
  • fig3_main_result.pdf, w3_latencies.json, w3_repeats.json, w3_fit.json saved
Weekend 4Device validation≈ 5 hours

Dynamic circuits on device noise

Run the code with real-time feed-forward on a calibrated replica of an IBM device (no account needed), or on the device itself, and measure what decoder latency costs.

The protocol

One job holds three circuits, each prepared in logical |1⟩, on one fixed physical layout:

  • bare — one physical qubit (the same one as data qubit 0) idling for exactly as long as the encoded circuit's encode-and-syndrome stage, using a delay the transpiler cannot remove;
  • offline — encoded, syndrome measured, no feed-forward; the syndrome is decoded afterwards in software, shot by shot;
  • realtime — encoded, syndrome measured, correction applied by three if_test blocks.

Four read-outs come from them: bare, majority vote alone, offline decode and real-time correction. The sweep mode inserts a wait of 0–80 µs between the syndrome readout and the correction, a stand-in for decoder latency that the replica's noise model can see.

Run it

python src/experiment_4_real_hardware.py local FakeKingston      # Heron r2 replica
python src/experiment_4_real_hardware.py local FakeSherbrooke    # Eagle r3 replica
python src/experiment_4_real_hardware.py sweep FakeKingston      # latency sweep
python src/experiment_4_real_hardware.py draw                    # the circuit figure
Reference run · 4,000 shots per circuit
Device replicaBareMajority onlyOffline decodeReal-timeReal-time − bareReal-time − offline
Heron r2 (FakeKingston)97.88%99.72%99.70%99.55%+1.68 pp, p = 6×10⁻¹¹−0.15 pp, p = 0.36
Eagle r3 (FakeSherbrooke)97.38%99.28%99.10%99.00%+1.62 pp, p = 8×10⁻⁸−0.10 pp, p = 0.73

The code helps clearly on both devices; real-time and offline correction tie because the replica adds no feed-forward delay. In one round that ends with reading the data qubits, a majority vote already undoes any single flip, so the syndrome adds nothing here; it matters when the state must survive further rounds.

Latency sweep. Logical error starts at 0.45% (Heron) and 1.00% (Eagle), doubles after a 7.6 µs and 12.8 µs wait, and reaches 5.6–5.7% at 40 µs. The 40 µs deadline is a ceiling, not a safe operating point: a correction that lands “on time” at 30 µs has already lost most of the code's benefit.

Real hardware

Save your API key once, then submit, and retrieve when the job is done. I haven't run this part on a real device yet, since it needs my IBM credentials. The job is 12,000 shots, well within the free Open Plan's 10 minutes per 28 days. On hardware, the real-time-versus-offline comparison includes the controller's true feed-forward latency, which no replica models.

python src/save_ibm_account.py
python src/experiment_4_real_hardware.py submit
python src/experiment_4_real_hardware.py retrieve <job_id>
API note. qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.50 deprecates SamplerV2; this script uses the client-side Sampler from qiskit_ibm_runtime.executor_sampler, with twirling and dynamical decoupling switched off so results are raw (decoupling cannot be combined with dynamic circuits anyway).

Weekend 4 checklist

  • Both replicas run; all three circuits share one layout (check the printed qubit lists)
  • Sweep run; doubling wait recorded
  • Optional: hardware job submitted, job ID in w4_job_manifest.json

Full statistical analysis

One script turns the Weekend 3 data into the final statistics: τ* with bootstrap intervals, tail diagnostics, the Python-versus-C test and a ready-to-paste LaTeX table.

Reference run
Tierτ* = P99, 95% CIHeadroom vs 40 µsHill αStalls > 1 µs
Python268 ns [248, 290]149×3.957 (median 13.1 µs)
C extension46 ns [45, 47]870×7.931 (23.0 µs)
Bare-metal (modelled)95 ns [95, 96]420×52.70

Python versus C: Mann–Whitney p < 10⁻³⁰⁰, rank-biserial r = +0.998, median ratio 3.6×. Below a survival probability of about 10⁻³ the curves leave the Hill fit and flatten into the stall plateau, so VR at large τ must be counted directly, never extrapolated from a fitted tail.
